personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Justin is established with a distinct, layered personality across multiple encounters. He is friendly, socially confident, and eager to belong: he introduces himself warmly to Harry, Hermione, and Ron by name in Herbology (Scene 3–4), demonstrates class-conscious pride in his Muggle background (references Eton, his mother's expectations, his family wanting a trained wizard), and shows enthusiastic if credulous admiration for Lockhart (Scene 6–7). He is also capable of fear-driven hostility: when he believes Harry is dangerous, he avoids him (Scene 9), storms out of the Duelling Club angrily after the snake incident (Scene 30), and hides in his dormitory on Ernie's advice (Scene 48). His voice is direct, sociable, and lightly upper-class in register ('My name was down for Eton, you know'). He can hold a grudge (avoiding Harry for weeks, laughing at him in Herbology in Book 3 over the Bouncing Bulbs), but also apologises sincerely and at length once cleared (Scene 84). He is not passive: he reacts, confronts, and then reconciles on his own terms.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the theatrical film, Justin's self-introduction scene before the Duelling Club has been cut per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction. This removes the only film moment where Justin speaks proactively, introduces himself, references Lockhart enthusiastically, and exhibits his sociable, class-tinged voice. What remains in the theatrical cut is: Justin standing near Harry at the Duelling Club where the snake is directed at him (he says one line: 'What are you playing at?' before backing away in terror), and a brief non-speaking appearance in the final feast scene where he rejoins the Hufflepuffs. The single retained line — 'What are you playing at?' — does preserve the fear-and-hostility response that is present in the books, but it strips it of the preceding context (the warm self-introduction, the Lockhart enthusiasm, the class pride) that gives it emotional texture. The film Justin is a near-silent victim figure with one reactive line.
personality_voice.difference: The books establish Justin as friendly, socially assertive, credulous about Lockhart, and class-conscious before he becomes fearful of Harry. The film removes all of this proactive personality and reduces him to a single frightened reaction. His voice, humor, social ease, Muggle-world pride, and Lockhart enthusiasm are entirely absent from what reaches the screen. The sustained pattern of avoidance followed by sincere reconciliation (Book 2 ending) and later the cold-shoulder behavior in Book 3 (Herbology scene) are also absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The loss of the self-introduction scene (cut from theatrical release) removes the primary evidence for Justin's personality and voice — his directness, warmth, class-conscious humor, and Lockhart credulity. What remains is one frightened reactive line. This is a substantial personality reduction: the character is recognisable as 'a Muggle-born student who fears Harry' but the traits that defined him beyond that function are absent. Score placed in the 10–13 range: personality is substantially altered in several important scenes, though 'What are you playing at?' does preserve at minimum his confrontational fear response from the books.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline across multiple scenes. Film portrayal directly evidenced by what remains in the theatrical cut (one line, one silent appearance). The cut introduction scene is excluded per instruction.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Justin serves several distinct narrative functions in the books. First, he is a named, individualised Muggle-born student whose fear of Harry makes the Chamber of Secrets threat personal and socially costly for Harry: Justin's avoidance after the snake incident (Scene 9), Ernie's conversation about him hiding in the dormitory (Scene 48), and Harry's active effort to find and clear his name with Justin (Scenes 44–55) all give Justin agency as a social antagonist whose suspicion Harry must navigate. Second, Justin is a victim of the Basilisk whose Petrification is a major plot beat (Scene 58–73) and whose eventual revival is a marker of the story's resolution (Scene 84). Third, in later books (Order of the Phoenix), Justin is a named DA member who participates in the defence against Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle on the Hogwarts Express (Scene 97), demonstrating active loyalty and agency as a trained fighter. Justin also provides Harry's connection to the broader Hufflepuff social world and to Muggle-born vulnerability as a theme.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, Justin's narrative role is reduced to: (1) being the person the snake is aimed at during the Duelling Club, triggering the Parseltongue revelation — a plot function he retains but does not actively drive; (2) lying Petrified in the corridor (a visual beat, no speech or agency); (3) silently rejoining the Hufflepuffs at the end-of-year feast. The DA subplot (Book 5) is absent from the film corpus provided, so the Order of the Phoenix material cannot be credited or evaluated here. The key agency loss is that Justin's role as a social obstacle Harry actively tries to resolve — the scenes where Harry seeks him out, confronts the Hufflepuffs, and tries to repair his reputation — is largely stripped. Ernie's conversation about Justin hiding is present in the film corpus (Scene 73 of the film), but Justin himself has no agency in any of these sequences in the theatrical cut.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The book Justin is both a passive victim and an active social agent whose suspicion Harry must work to overcome. The film Justin is only a passive victim and an incidental trigger for the Parseltongue revelation. His role as a figure Harry pursues and must clear his name with is present in the screenplay but entirely through Ernie's dialogue — Justin himself never appears in those scenes with any lines or action.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Justin's core plot function (Petrification victim, Parseltongue trigger) is preserved. However, his agency as a social antagonist — the scenes requiring Harry to seek him out and address his suspicion — is absent from what Justin himself does on screen. The role is partially present through other characters' dialogue about him (Ernie), but Justin's own agency in that dynamic is gone. This is a meaningful reduction: the character's narrative role is recognisable but materially weakened. Score in the 10–13 range.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced by absence of Justin's lines/actions in relevant scenes.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Justin's motivations are clear and consistent in the books. He is a Muggle-born who is proud of his background and has actively chosen the wizarding world (Eton reference, converting his mother), but that background also makes him vulnerable: once the Chamber of Secrets attacks begin, fear for his safety motivates his hostility toward Harry. His internal conflict is mild but present: he wants to belong to the wizarding world and trust its heroes (he was friendly with Harry before), but his fear and the plausible-seeming evidence (Parseltongue, Slytherin's heir) override that. This conflict resolves in his sincere apology at the feast. He also has a brief social-pressure dimension: Ernie's group gossip shapes his behavior, suggesting susceptibility to peer influence alongside his personal fear.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, Justin's motivations are inferrable only from his one line and his Petrification. The fear motivation is present in 'What are you playing at?' but the fuller picture — his pride in being Muggle-born, the specific conflict between his earlier friendliness toward Harry and his subsequent fear, the peer-pressure element, and the resolution through apology — is absent. The film never shows why Justin in particular fears Harry beyond being the person the snake approached.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The motivation (fear as a Muggle-born) is partially present by implication but is not developed or complicated. The internal conflict between prior friendliness and current fear, and the resolution of that conflict, are absent. What remains is fear without texture.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivation (Muggle-born fear of the heir) survives in implication, but it is underexplained and the internal conflict (prior warmth vs. current fear, personal resolution) is absent. This is a partial alteration — the motivation is not opposite or absent, but it is flattened significantly. Score in the 8–10 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal: reasonably inferred from the single line and Petrification scene.

character_arc.book_baseline: Justin has a small but coherent arc across Book 2: starting point is friendly openness toward Harry and the wizarding world, with class-conscious optimism; mid-arc is fear-driven hostility and avoidance after the Parseltongue incident; resolution is sincere public apology and reconciliation at the end-of-year feast. The arc is compact but complete: he begins trusting, becomes suspicious, and ends apologetic. In Book 3, a brief relapse into coldness over the Bouncing Bulbs (Scene 85) adds a small realistic complication. The arc is not dramatic, but it has a clear shape.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film does not show the opening friendliness (cut), so the starting point of the arc is absent. The fear response is present (Duelling Club). The resolution — Justin's apology and handshake — is absent from the theatrical cut: Justin is shown silently rejoining Hufflepuffs at the feast, but there is no apology scene. The arc is therefore truncated at both ends: no warm beginning, no reconciliation. What remains is only the fearful middle.
character_arc.difference: Starting point (friendly, optimistic Muggle-born) and resolution (sincere apology, reconciliation) are both absent. The arc is reduced to a single moment of fear with no before or after.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is missing its beginning and its resolution. The character's journey from trust to fear to reconciliation — which is the entirety of his meaningful arc in Book 2 — is reduced to fear only. This is an incomplete, rushed presentation that removes important steps. Score in the 8–10 range.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced by what is present and absent in theatrical scenes.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Justin's most important relationship in the books is with Harry: it begins as open admiration and social warmth, curdles into fear-based hostility, and resolves into apologetic reconciliation. This relationship is important because it shows Harry's social cost during the Chamber of Secrets crisis and humanises Justin as someone who must overcome fear to do the right thing. Justin's relationship with Ernie Macmillan is also relevant: Ernie shapes Justin's fear response and speaks for him, suggesting Justin is part of a peer group where he defers to Ernie's more extreme suspicion. In Order of the Phoenix, Justin's relationship with Harry takes a positive turn as a DA member who fights alongside him.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, Justin and Harry never share a meaningful exchange after the snake incident. Justin backs away in terror and that is the last direct contact. The apology — which is the emotional resolution of their relationship — is absent. The Ernie dynamic exists in the film (Ernie talks about Justin hiding) but Justin himself has no lines in that context. The relationship is present only as a one-sided fear reaction.
key_relationships.difference: The dynamic, arc, and resolution of the Harry-Justin relationship are absent from the theatrical film. What survives is only the fear beat. The reconciliation that defines the relationship's final state is gone. The Ernie peer-group dynamic is partially present but entirely mediated through Ernie, not Justin.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The emotional dynamic of the Harry-Justin relationship — warm start, fearful middle, reconciling end — is reduced to the fearful middle only. This substantially changes how the relationship reads. The peer-group dimension with Ernie is technically present but entirely off-screen from Justin's side. Score in the 3–4 range: key relationships are heavily flattened.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Justin's complexity in the books comes from several layered elements: (1) the class-conscious Muggle pride (Eton reference, converting his mother) that makes him a specific, textured individual rather than a generic Muggle-born; (2) the Lockhart enthusiasm that shows his credulity and social optimism; (3) the specific shame and social pressure of hiding in the dormitory rather than confronting Harry directly; (4) his eventual courage in apologising publicly and sincerely at the feast; (5) the brief Book 3 relapse into coldness (Bouncing Bulbs scene) that shows residual embarrassment rather than clean resolution; (6) his active DA participation and loyalty in Order of the Phoenix. Together these give Justin a personality that exceeds his plot function.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: In the theatrical cut, almost all of this material is absent. The Eton reference and class pride are gone (introduction scene cut). The Lockhart credulity is gone (same scene cut). The hiding-in-dormitory dynamic is present in the film corpus through Ernie's dialogue but Justin himself is absent from that sequence. The public apology is gone. The Book 3 Herbology relapse is not in scope here. The DA material is not in the provided film corpus. What survives is one frightened line and a silent background appearance.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The entirety of what makes Justin a character beyond 'Muggle-born victim' has been removed from the theatrical cut: his social voice, his class-conscious humor, his credulity about Lockhart, his peer-group dynamics, and his reconciliation. The lost introduction scene was the primary carrier of almost all his personality texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is reduced to a near-silent victim function. The material that distinguished Justin as an individual — rather than an interchangeable Muggle-born student — is almost entirely absent. This is major flattening into a single function. Score in the 5–7 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for book baseline. Film portrayal directly evidenced by theatrical absence of key scenes.

comparative.key_observations: Justin Finch-Fletchley is a case where a single scene excision — his Herbology/Duelling Club self-introduction, excluded from the theatrical release — strips away almost everything that made him a distinct character in the books. What survives theatrically is one frightened reactive line ('What are you playing at?') and a silent appearance at the end-of-year feast. His book characterisation rests on several interlocking elements: the warm, class-conscious, Lockhart-credulous personality established in Herbology; his role as a social obstacle Harry must actively pursue and reconcile with; the arc from trust through fear to apology; and the peer-group dynamics with Ernie. All of these are absent or reduced to near-zero in the theatrical film. The Petrification plot function and the Parseltongue-trigger function are both retained, but these are structural uses of Justin rather than characterisation of him. The result is a character who is recognisable in broad outline (Muggle-born student, afraid of Harry, Petrified) but has been functionally hollowed out. The score of 51 reflects that the core plot role is intact but the character beneath it has been almost entirely lost.
